title: 资源分配与阶段检查 · Four listening sections
instructions: 原创模拟训练材料；先独立作答，再核对依据。四节音频共40题，按顺序听音作答。合成训练音频时长不同于正式考试。
transcript:
Section 1: The Community Garden Meeting

Mia: Hi, thanks for coming to the community garden meeting. I'm Mia, the garden coordinator. Are you new here?
Ben: Yes, I'm Ben. I moved into the area last month. I'd like to help with the garden.
Mia: Great! We always need volunteers. What kind of work would you like to do?
Ben: I enjoy planting, but I'm not very good at planning. I usually just plant things and hope they grow.
Mia: That's fine. We have a planning team too. But let's talk about resources first. We have a small budget this year.
Ben: How much is the budget?
Mia: It's two hundred pounds for the whole year. We need to decide how to spend it.
Ben: That's not much. What do we need most?
Mia: Well, we need seeds, tools, and water. The water bill is the biggest cost. Last year it was eighty pounds.
Ben: Eighty pounds for water? That's a lot.
Mia: Yes, but we can save water if we collect rain. We could buy a water butt for fifty pounds.
Ben: A water butt? What's that?
Mia: It's a big container that collects rain from the roof. Then we can use that water for the plants.
Ben: That sounds like a good idea. But fifty pounds is a quarter of our budget.
Mia: True. But it will save money next year. Also, we need to check our progress. We should have a stage check every three months.
Ben: A stage check? What do you mean?
Mia: I mean we look at what we planned, what we did, and what we need to change. For example, in spring we plant, in summer we check if the plants are growing well.
Ben: That makes sense. So when is the next stage check?
Mia: It's at the end of June. We'll look at the water butt then. If we buy it, we'll see if it works.
Ben: OK. And what about tools? Do we need new ones?
Mia: We have some old tools, but they are broken. We need to buy a new spade. That costs fifteen pounds.
Ben: Fifteen pounds for a spade? That's cheap.
Mia: Yes, it's a good price. We also need gloves. A pair of gloves costs five pounds. We need four pairs, so that's twenty pounds.
Ben: So that's thirty-five pounds for tools and gloves.
Mia: Yes. And seeds? We can buy seeds for twenty pounds.
Ben: So if we buy the water butt, tools, gloves, and seeds, how much is that?
Mia: Let's see. Water butt fifty, spade fifteen, gloves twenty, seeds twenty. That's one hundred and five pounds. We have ninety-five pounds left.
Ben: That's good. We can save the rest for next year.
Mia: Exactly. But we also need to think about people. We have ten volunteers, but only five come regularly.
Ben: Why don't the others come?
Mia: Some are busy, some forget. We could send a reminder message.
Ben: That's a good idea. I can help with that.
Mia: Thanks, Ben. So, to sum up: we'll buy the water butt, a spade, gloves, and seeds. We'll have a stage check in June. And we'll send reminders to volunteers.
Ben: Sounds like a plan. I'm happy to help.

Section 2: Community Garden Meeting: Allocating Resources and Checking Progress

Chair: Good evening, everyone. Thanks for coming to the monthly meeting of the Green Roots Community Garden. I'm Lisa, the chair. Tonight we need to decide how to allocate our resources for the next three months and check our progress so far. Let's start with the budget. We have 500 dollars left for the season. Last month we spent 200 dollars on seeds and tools. So we have 300 dollars now. But we also need to pay for water. The water bill was 80 dollars last month. If we don't reduce water use, we will spend too much. So I suggest we buy a water tank. It costs 150 dollars. That leaves 150 dollars for other things. What do you think?

Tom: I'm Tom, the treasurer. I agree with the water tank. But we also need to fix the fence. The fence is broken in two places. Repairing it will cost 100 dollars. If we buy the tank and fix the fence, we will have only 50 dollars left. That might not be enough for seeds.

Lisa: Good point, Tom. But we already have some seeds donated by the school. So we don't need to buy many seeds. We can use the 50 dollars for small tools. Does that work?

Tom: Yes, that works. But we should also check our progress. Last season we grew 20 kilograms of tomatoes. This season we have already grown 15 kilograms. That's good, but we planned to grow 30 kilograms. So we are behind on tomatoes. However, we have grown more beans than planned. We planned 10 kilograms and we have 12 kilograms. So beans are ahead.

Lisa: Thanks, Tom. Now, about the work schedule. We need volunteers for watering. If we have a water tank, we can water less often. But we still need someone to check the plants every day. Mary, can you organize the watering schedule?

Mary: Sure, I can do that. But I need to know who is available. I'll send an email to all members. If people reply by Friday, I can make the schedule by Sunday. Also, we should have a work day next Saturday. We can fix the fence then. If we have enough people, we can finish in one day.

Lisa: Great. So to summarize: we will buy a water tank for 150 dollars, fix the fence for 100 dollars, and use 50 dollars for tools. Mary will organize watering and a work day. We will check progress again next month. Any questions?

Tom: Just one. What about the compost? We have a lot of compost, but we need to turn it. If we don't turn it, it won't be ready for next season.

Lisa: Good catch. We can add that to the work day. If we have time, we will turn the compost. If not, we will do it the following week. Okay, let's vote. All in favor? (Several voices: Aye.) Opposed? (Silence.) Great, the plan is approved. Thank you all for coming.

Section 3: Allocating Resources for the Student Garden Project

Tutor: Good morning, Li and Wang. Today we're allocating resources for the student garden. We have a budget of £500 for this term. Please explain your priorities before we agree on the figures.
Li: I think we should prioritize buying seeds and tools first. Without them, we can't start. If we buy high-quality seeds, we'll have a better harvest. We should also leave some money for gloves and watering cans.
Wang: Seeds are essential, but we need somewhere dry for the tools. Renting a shed might cost around £150 per month, which is too expensive. Perhaps we could build a wooden storage box instead.
Tutor: A box would cost less. We also need soil and fertilizer. What would you allow for those?
Li: I suggest £100 for soil and fertilizer. If we use compost from the school cafeteria, we can reduce the cost. Its composting scheme produces finished compost that we can get for free. That would save us at least £50.
Wang: We should test it first. If it contains too much salt, it could harm the plants. Free material isn't useful if it damages the garden.
Tutor: Agreed. Let's allocate £50 for testing the compost. Now, the old tools are rusty. Repairing them would cost about £30, while replacing them all would cost £120.
Li: Repairing is cheaper and creates less waste. We could spend the savings on a rain barrel to collect water.
Wang: Rusty tools might break easily and cause injuries. Could we buy a few new essential tools and repair the rest?
Tutor: That balances cost and safety. Let's allocate £60 for a mix of repairing and buying a few new tools. How much do we need for publicity?
Li: I think £40 is enough for posters and flyers. We can design them ourselves and print them on recycled paper at the school print shop.
Wang: We can also create a free online sign-up form. Sharing it through student groups would reach people who miss the posters.
Tutor: Good. The budget will be £100 for seeds, £60 for tools, £100 for soil and fertilizer, £50 for compost testing, £40 for publicity, and £50 for a rain barrel. That totals £400, leaving £100 as a contingency fund for unexpected costs.
Li: We should keep receipts, so we can compare actual spending with the plan.
Tutor: Exactly. We'll have a progress check in four weeks. We'll review spending and plant growth then. If we overspend early, we'll have less for later stages.
Wang: If the seeds don't germinate within two weeks, we might need to buy new ones. We must also see the compost test results before using it. Buying fertilizer instead could cost extra.
Li: I'll monitor the compost test and report back. When do we confirm the plan?
Tutor: Next Friday. That is a planning meeting, separate from the progress check. Please bring your ideas for installing the rain barrel.

Section 4: Resource Allocation and Stage Checks in a Community Garden Project

Good morning, everyone. Today I want to talk about how we managed resources and checked progress in a community garden project. This is a simulated case study, not a real project, but the lessons are useful for any small team. Let me start with the background. Last year, our local community centre received a small grant to turn an unused car park into a garden. We had twelve volunteers and a budget of five thousand pounds. The project lasted six months, from March to August. We divided the work into three stages: planning, building, and growing. At the end of each stage, we held a review meeting to check if we were on track. Now, let me explain how we allocated our resources. First, we spent about forty percent of the budget on materials, such as wood for raised beds and soil. Second, we allocated twenty percent for tools, like spades and watering cans. Third, we set aside fifteen percent for seeds and plants. The remaining twenty-five percent covered unexpected costs, such as repairing a fence and buying extra compost. We also allocated volunteer time carefully. Each volunteer worked four hours a week, usually on Saturday mornings. We used a simple sign-up sheet to avoid having too many people on one day. Now, about stage checks. After the planning stage, we reviewed our design and realised we had forgotten to include a water tap. So we adjusted the plan and added a tap near the entrance. This was a small change but it saved a lot of time later. After the building stage, we checked the raised beds and found that two of them were not level. We fixed them before planting. At the final stage, we checked the plants and found that the tomatoes were growing well, but the lettuce was not. We learned that lettuce needs more shade, so next time we will plant it in a different spot. One important lesson was about communication. At first, we sent emails, but many volunteers did not read them. So we started using a messaging app, and attendance improved. Another lesson was about flexibility. We had planned to buy ready-made compost, but it was too expensive. Instead, we made our own compost from kitchen waste, which was cheaper and better for the environment. Now, let me summarise the key points. First, allocate resources based on priorities and keep a reserve for unexpected costs. Second, check your progress at the end of each stage and be ready to adjust. Third, communicate in a way that suits your team. These lessons can apply to many projects, not just gardens. Thank you for listening. I'm happy to take questions at the end, but for now, let's move on to the next part.

grammar.title: 条件句；数量词；指代与衔接
grammar.explanation: 条件句用 if 表示“如果……就……”。真实条件句：if + 一般现在时，主句用 will/can 等。例如：If we buy it, we'll see if it works. 数量词如 a pair of, a quarter of, how much, how many。指代与衔接：用 it, they, this, that 等指代前文，使段落连贯。
grammar.example: If we buy it, we'll see if it works.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
options: If it rains, we will stay at home.
If it will rain, we stay at home.
If it rains, we stayed at home.
If it rained, we will stay at home.
answers: If it rains, we will stay at home.
questions.explanation: 真实条件句中，if 从句用一般现在时，主句用 will + 动词原形。
questions.evidence: If we buy it, we'll see if it works.

questions.prompt: Complete the sentence with one word: We need three ______ of shoes. (pair/pairs)

questions.evidence: We need four pairs, so that's twenty pounds.

questions.evidence: We could buy a water butt for fifty pounds. It will save money.
